slides.title: Sector Exposure & Executive Risk Outlook
slides.decision: Treat B&PW cyber risk as a concentration and counterparty-liquidity issue.
slides.visual_type: Judgement table with confidence and change conditions

elements.visible_text: The best-documented Building & Public Works cyber propagation runs through shared digital layers - owner shared services, sector platforms, cloud hosting, materials suppliers and payment chains - and reaches the financial system mainly through contractor liquidity, not direct loss.

Public records for the reporting period across the EU, EEA and UK with global comparison: five named incidents; council, auditor, regulator, state and stock-exchange disclosures; two ransomware leak-site datasets; official insolvency statistics.

Construction ranks among the most frequently claimed ransomware victim groups: 176 of 1,140 industrial claims in the latest published quarter and third across all sectors over 12 months. The best-documented disruption hit a public project owner, halting planning for about 15 weeks and constraining invoice processing.

slides.title: Key Threats & Top 5 Cyber Attacks
slides.decision: Distinguish patterns from named incidents and prioritise pathways with propagation.

elements.visible_text: Five incidents in the period meet the evidence standard, but only two hit a contractor or materials supplier: owner, supplier and operational-technology pathways matter as much as direct ransomware against contractors.

Threat pathways (patterns, not attacks): P1 ransomware and data extortion; P2 phishing and edge or VPN access without multi-factor authentication; P3 shared IT and software-as-a-service dependency; P4 internet-exposed operational technology (OT) and building systems; P5 payment-chain fraud on supplier invoices.

Phishing (about 60%) and vulnerability exploitation (about 21%) dominate initial access in the latest EU cross-sector baseline, which pre-dates the period. Materials suppliers are repeatedly targeted because of reliance on enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and tight timelines. A national authority warned of opportunistic Iranian targeting of exposed infrastructure; unattributed US water OT activity followed.

Femern Link Contractors (Fehmarnbelt tunnel) Infrastructure construction; Denmark and Germany Owner confirmed incident; media report network shutdown, access-control loss, idle vessels Owner statement; effects unconfirmed
row_cells: Owner confirmed incident; media report network shutdown, access-control loss, idle vessels

row_cells: Planning, repairs, finance and revenues disrupted; data exfiltrated

elements.visible_text: Weight counterparty reviews towards propagation pathways - shared services, platforms, suppliers and exposed OT - rather than counting contractor ransomware claims alone.

Fehmarnbelt effects are media-reported; attribution of the US water activity is preliminary; private contractor victims seen only on leak sites were excluded, so contractor incidents are under-counted.

slides.executive_conclusion: Five incidents in the period meet the evidence standard, but only two hit a contractor or materials supplier: owner, supplier and operational-technology pathways matter as much as direct ransomware against contractors.

slides.title: Financial Impact: Building & Public Works
slides.decision: Use time and liquidity, not summed losses, as the financial lens.

elements.visible_text: Public financial evidence is thin and cannot be added up: in-period quantified outcomes come from one public owner and one regulator, and the evidence suggests time is the main cost driver - weeks of site downtime and months of owner process disruption.

Benchmarks: about 24 days average ransomware downtime in construction (insurer research, method undisclosed); council cyber costs of GBP 1.2 million in one financial year; SEK 1.8 million GDPR fine on a public-sector software supplier; historical GBP 4.4 million UK fine on a construction group.

Transmission to banks is conditional: owner payment delays strain contractor working capital; construction already records the highest insolvency count in England and Wales; payment-diversion fraud targets stage payments; a government-guaranteed bank loan was provided to support a manufacturer's supply chain after a cyber stoppage.
Project delay Reported idle vessels on a major tunnel programme; 24-day downtime benchmark Indicated, not quantified

slides.executive_conclusion: Public financial evidence is thin and cannot be added up: in-period quantified outcomes come from one public owner and one regulator, and the evidence suggests time is the main cost driver - weeks of site downtime and months of owner process disruption.

slides.title: Case Study: Kensington and Chelsea Shared-IT Cyber Attack
slides.decision: Use the case as a recovery benchmark for owner-side disruption.

elements.visible_text: An intrusion into IT shared by three London boroughs, attributed by the auditor to human error, halted planning for about 15 weeks and revenues and benefits for about six months and constrained invoice processing, showing how owner-side disruption reaches contractors that depend on consents and payments.

Evidence base: council decision, scrutiny and audit-committee reports, the external auditor's annual report and the council's public FAQ; selected because it is the only case in the period with full chronology, disclosed cost and auditor findings.

Cause and constraint: the auditor attributes the incident to human error and slow recovery to a fragmented legacy estate. Disruption came from containing and rebuilding shared systems, not from attacker encryption.
Detection Day 0 Unusual activity; emergency command; shared systems isolated
row_cells: Unusual activity; emergency command; shared systems isolated

elements.visible_text: Notification Days 3-28 Data exfiltration confirmed; regulator notified twice; police investigation
row_cells: Data exfiltration confirmed; regulator notified twice; police investigation

elements.visible_text: Containment Weeks 1-7 Manual workarounds; controlled run paid more than GBP 5 million of invoices
row_cells: Manual workarounds; controlled run paid more than GBP 5 million of invoices

elements.visible_text: Phased reopening Months 2-4 Finance and HR restored; planning system back after about 15 weeks
row_cells: Finance and HR restored; planning system back after about 15 weeks

elements.visible_text: Revenues restart About month 6 Benefits and revenues restart; local tax bills issued late
row_cells: Benefits and revenues restart; local tax bills issued late

elements.visible_text: Assurance About month 10 GBP 1.2 million costs in the year; auditor reports governance weakness
row_cells: GBP 1.2 million costs in the year; auditor reports governance weakness

elements.visible_text: Transferable lesson: shared-service models concentrate risk across authorities; consents, instructions and supplier payments are the owner functions that drive contractor activity.
Treat owner digital disruption as foreseeable in contractor cash-flow and contract planning, and ask public-owner counterparties how they would certify and pay during a multi-month outage.
The case does not show quantified contractor losses, project delay, the initial access vector or insurance recovery; it concerns one UK local-authority shared service.

slides.executive_conclusion: An intrusion into IT shared by three London boroughs, attributed by the auditor to human error, halted planning for about 15 weeks and revenues and benefits for about six months and constrained invoice processing, showing how owner-side disruption reaches contractors that depend on consents and payments.

slides.title: Systemic Dependencies & Regulatory Outlook
slides.decision: Recognise indirect legal reach and unregulated concentration.
slides.visual_type: Dependency chains and regulatory status matrix

elements.visible_text: Construction is not a listed sector under the EU NIS2 Directive, the EU CER Directive on entity resilience or the UK NIS Regulations, so obligations arrive indirectly - through owners' supply-chain duties, procurement terms, product rules and data protection - while shared platforms and suppliers create concentration that no regime addresses directly.

Evidenced dependency chains: owner shared IT -> planning, repairs and payment; public-sector SaaS -> most municipalities in one country; construction-management SaaS -> third-party cloud; materials suppliers -> ERP-dependent supply; public-works operational technology -> many small operators; stage payments -> invoice fraud.

Pressure is rising in the period: product reporting duties started, entity identification under CER fell due, an EU procurement reform with cyber and resilience terms was proposed, and four Member States were taken to court over NIS2.
NIS2 Binding via national law Water, road and public-administration owners pass supply-chain duties to contractors
row_cells: Water, road and public-administration owners pass supply-chain duties to contractors

elements.visible_text: CER Directive Binding via national law Designated operators can impose resilience terms on construction suppliers
row_cells: Designated operators can impose resilience terms on construction suppliers

row_cells: Reporting duty now applies to building-automation and site-product makers

National NIS2 scope extensions were not surveyed exhaustively; the bill and the proposal may change; construction platform market shares are not public.

slides.executive_conclusion: Construction is not a listed sector under the EU NIS2 Directive, the EU CER Directive on entity resilience or the UK NIS Regulations, so obligations arrive indirectly - through owners' supply-chain duties, procurement terms, product rules and data protection - while shared platforms and suppliers create concentration that no regime addresses directly.

slides.title: Mitigation Strategies & Security Framework
slides.decision: Assign evidence-linked priorities with completion evidence and triggers.

elements.visible_text: Six evidence-linked priorities address the five pathways: map shared dependencies, harden identity and remote access, segregate operational technology (OT) and site systems, confirm payment changes, align contractual flow-down and test manual fallback for time-sensitive works.
A1 Shared dependencies (0-6 months) Which owners, platforms and cloud regions do top sector counterparties rely on? Dependency map; continuity test results Provider outage or breach notice

elements.visible_text: Evidence base: state recommendations for OT, a joint ransomware advisory, the EU threat baseline, a law-enforcement fraud alert, insurer research and the case study.
Frameworks are reference vocabularies, not law: NIST CSF 2.0 Govern and Recover, ISO 19650-5 for built-asset information and IEC 62443 for OT.
Give each priority a 1LoD owner and a dated completion artefact, and escalate to the Risk Committee when a monitoring trigger fires.
Actions are sector priorities drawn from public evidence, not findings about any institution's controls, losses or risk appetite.

slides.executive_conclusion: Six evidence-linked priorities address the five pathways: map shared dependencies, harden identity and remote access, segregate operational technology (OT) and site systems, confirm payment changes, align contractual flow-down and test manual fallback for time-sensitive works.
